doc.title: Ira Gitler interviewed by Michael Woods, New York City, New York, November 16, 1995

title: Learning by ear, Parker, and the Steeple Chase riff
summary: Without method books beyond Arban, musicians absorbed what they heard; Gitler cites Parker's memory, Steeple Chase's theme from Lunceford's Margie, and Laughin' Louie.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Reading music versus faking and playing by ear

blocks.x: You know this is something I also want you to comment on. You know at the time that Louis was in his heyday one of the things that many students going to music schools now don’t realize, there were no method books.
Well there was the Arban book I guess, I don’t know when that came in, you know.
Well that didn’t explain any jazz harmonies though.

No, no, it just was for technique. No. I think he listened and he heard, and most of the great musicians, no matter how much training they have and put that in their service, it’s the intuitive and what they soak up and play back at you. You know Charlie Parker was amazing the way he would hear fragments of songs or whole songs, and incorporate them. He just was omnivorous in his listening, you could see. And an incredible retentive memory, as we know from the way he would change his solos from take to take on a particular number. But I don’t know if I talked about this when I was up to your class, but it was something I discovered a couple of years ago, that his “Steeple Chase,” the theme of his song “Steeple Chase” was taken from a riff that was used behind Trummy Young’s vocal of “Margie” with Jimmie Lunceford. And it was a record that sold a lot of copies and had a lot of exposure, and everyone who came up in that period heard it, and obviously Charlie Parker heard it too, and it was just a little phrase that they play when he’s taking a breath. And Charlie Parker took that phrase and, you know, made a whole tune out of it. That’s just one little example. So I think, getting back to Louis Armstrong, I think he heard all the music that was happening around him. Ragtime, the blues, opera, you know, light classical as they used to call it, and the classics. But I think opera was very popular then and I think a lot of people heard operatic themes and in fact I think some of those type of pieces were used as things to warm up on, you know to practice with. ‘Cause there’s a record called “Laughin’ Louie,” I don’t know if you know that record, it’s a novelty, and Louis’ having a good time in the studio with everybody and people are cracking up in between, after the vocal, and then he says, “Here’s one of those good old good ones,” and no one’s ever been able to tell me what it is and I don’t know.
But it kind of has that semi-classical as we used to call it, light opera or whatever, it’s a theme like that. And he plays that and does a lot of miraculous things with it.
